tier_reason: The csv-parser benchmarks/README.md raw-throughput table carries every number in the record; the harness is public (vincentlaucsb/csv-parser benchmarks/fast_cpp_csv_parser_read_bench.cpp vs benchmarks/csv_parser_read_bench.cpp, built by benchmarks/CMakeLists.txt with Google Benchmark v1.8.5), compiler MSVC 19.50, flags derivable from public build files (CMake Release config, /arch:AVX2 added by csv-parser's top-level CMakeLists.txt on MSVC), CPU i5-12400. Third-party (competitor) run, so A holds.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Single-parser-worker raw read, median real time (csv-parser vs fast-cpp-csv-parser): 500K clean count 146.5 ms vs 81.8 ms (~1.8x, derived from page data), read 164.9 ms vs 82.8 ms (~2.0x, derived from page data); 500K quoted count 197.2 ms vs 118.8 ms (~1.7x, derived from page data), read 223.5 ms vs 136.2 ms (~1.6x, derived from page data); 5M clean read 1,087 ms vs 944.2 ms (~1.15x, derived from page data). Reversed at 5M rows elsewhere: 5M clean count 547.6 ms for csv-parser vs 881.5 ms, 5M quoted count 665.4 ms vs 1,153 ms, 5M quoted read 1,140 ms vs 1,164 ms (csv-parser ahead). csv-parser also wins both materialization tables (e.g. 5M clean 739.6 ms vs 2,105 ms) and the positional-read table once it uses 4+ speculative parser workers (500K clean spec-4 76.6 ms vs fast-cpp SPSC 88.0 ms).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: MSVC 19.50 (Visual Studio 2026), Windows SDK 10.0.26100.0, C++20, CMake Release configuration (MSVC Release defaults; no extra optimization flags in benchmarks/CMakeLists.txt), /arch:AVX2 added to CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS by csv-parser's top-level CMakeLists.txt on MSVC (in csv-parser's own directory scope, so the fast-cpp benchmark executables in benchmarks/ probably build without it), CSV_ENABLE_THREADS=ON, Google Benchmark 1.8.5
corrections.caveats: The benchmark is in the competitor's repo (csv-parser author), not the project's own, and it was written to show where csv-parser wins: fast-cpp-csv-parser wins only at 500K rows and the 5M clean read, and loses the 5M count rows (clean and quoted), the 5M quoted read, both materialization tables and the 4+ worker positional-read comparison. The two read harnesses do different work: fast-cpp's 'count rows' still copies all 8 fields into std::string per row while csv-parser's count only iterates rows, and fast-cpp's 'read' copies all 8 fields while csv-parser takes 3 string_views by column name; fast-cpp is configured with double_quote_escape and trim_chars even on the clean profile. Windows/MSVC only, one machine, Google Benchmark overhead included. The fast-cpp-csv-parser source is fetched with FetchContent GIT_TAG master, so no commit is pinned (the repo has not changed since 2025-02-02). Optimization flags are implied by CMake Release rather than listed. fast-cpp-csv-parser cannot parse quoted line breaks (multiline profile skipped). The project's own README has no numbers, and no measurement against the guessed std::getline baseline was found (dfglib's csvPerformanceRuns.md only compares it with dfglib's own readers).

notes: Numbers check out row by row; the record omitted that fast-cpp also loses the 5M quoted count and read, now added. Count/read harnesses are not identical (fast-cpp copies all 8 fields into std::string, csv-parser does not), which if anything handicaps fast-cpp. Metadata verified on github.com: BSD-3-Clause LICENSE, 2.4k stars, 438 forks, not a fork, last commit 2025-02-02 (stale). The category's baseline list names 'csv-parser libs the benchmark names', so baseline_in_list could be argued true; left unchanged.

tier_reason: The only numbers are the flex author's own 1988 timings against AT&T lex (Sun 3/60, 28,088-line C input), which three WebSearch queries attribute to comp.compilers article 88-04-001 (a reply by Vern Paxson); compilers.iecc.com is EGRESS_BLOCKED, so they are snippet only. First-party, no benchmark code, no compiler or flags: C at most, and nothing in the repository (README, NEWS, ONEWS, doc/flex.texi) carries lex timings.

corrections.claimed_speedup: AT&T lex 29.8 s vs flex 19.3 s with default table compression (~1.5x, derived from page data), 9.0 s with flex -cfe (~3.3x, derived from page data) and 7.8 s with flex -cf (~3.8x, derived from page data); times are user + system CPU and exclude identifier hashing. Snippet only: read from WebSearch result text for comp.compilers 88-04-001, page not opened.
corrections.workload: Generated C-language tokenizer (recognizing keywords, which the post says maximizes flex's advantage) run over a 28,088-line, 685K-character C input on a Sun 3/60 in April 1988; user + system CPU time, identifier hashing excluded (snippet only).
corrections.stars_or_usage: 4.0k stars, 568 forks; standard scanner generator shipped by Linux and BSD distributions
corrections.caveats: SNIPPET ONLY: the lex vs flex timings come from WebSearch result text attributed to comp.compilers article 88-04-001 ('Re: replacements for LEX: flex, ... , Rex', April 1988, described in the snippet as a reply by Vern Paxson, flex's author, so first-party); article 90-11-063 ('Re: Flex speed') also surfaced and may repeat the same 'old timings'. compilers.iecc.com is blocked by the egress proxy, so the page was never opened and the attribution is not pinned beyond the snippets. Timings are from 1988 hardware, 1988 flex and AT&T lex, with 1988 option syntax. The flex repository (README, NEWS, ONEWS, doc/flex.texi) contains no lex timings; its manual only says -f/-F is 'much faster (factor of 2-3)' than -C (flex against itself) and that -l AT&T-lex compatibility costs performance. Search snippets also say re2c -b scanners are faster than flex -Cf ones. COPYING is flex's own BSD-style text (two numbered conditions plus a no-endorsement paragraph, functionally BSD-3-Clause); GitHub does not identify it and the awesome-c list tags it BSD-2-Clause.

notes: Kept at C instead of the null-URL D rule because three separate WebSearch queries returned the exact same numbers attributed to comp.compilers 88-04-001; benchmark_url set to that article, but it was NOT opened (EGRESS_BLOCKED) and page_compares/numbers_found are null for that reason; a session with compilers.iecc.com access should confirm the article or drop the tier to D. Metadata verified on github.com: 4.0k stars, 568 forks, not a fork, not archived, last commit 2026-07-30 (active), COPYING read. Notable regardless of tier (standard lex replacement).

tier_reason: Upgraded C to B: cmark's own benchmarks.md (tags 0.21.0 to 0.29.0) lists hoedown 0.21 s vs cmark 0.29 s and discount 1.85 s, measured by the CommonMark team (independent of hoedown, and a competitor reporting a loss) with a public harness (cmark Makefile 'bench' target, bench/stats.py, Pro Git input). Not A: no compiler or flags, CPU given only as 'Intel Core 2 Duo at 2GHz', hoedown version unstated.

corrections.claimed_speedup: cmark benchmarks.md (tags 0.21.0 to 0.29.0): hoedown 0.21 s vs cmark 0.29 s (~1.4x, derived from page data) and vs discount 1.85 s (~8.8x, derived from page data) on the same table; at tag 0.20.0 the table read hoedown 0.21 s vs cmark 0.35 s. why-cmark-and-not-x.md repeats 'slightly faster than cmark in our benchmarks (0.21s vs. 0.29s)'.
corrections.workload: Markdown to HTML conversion of an 11 MB file built by concatenating all localizations of the first edition of Pro Git, timed by cmark's 'make bench PROG=...' target with time -p (time with empty input subtracted to remove startup, median of ten runs, process reniced).
corrections.hardware: ancient Thinkpad, Intel Core 2 Duo at 2GHz (exact model not stated)
corrections.caveats: Numbers are from the cmark team's benchmark (a competing project), circa 2015 (hoedown 3.x era; the table does not name versions), and were dropped from cmark's benchmarks.md at tag 0.30.0; the current page uses a 1106 KB input on a 2.3GHz 8-core i9 MacBook Pro and lists only commonmark.js, cmark and md4c, and cmark has been optimized since. No compiler or flags for any implementation. hoedown implements original Markdown plus extensions, not CommonMark, so the two produce different output for the same input. why-cmark-and-not-x.md reports hoedown taking 17.84 s on a 50000-deep nested bracket input where cmark took 0.073 s user time, and lists many parsing bugs as of hoedown v3.0.3. The README's own claim ('up to 40 times faster than other native alternatives' when wrapped in Python or Ruby) names no baseline and has no data. Repository dormant since 2015-12-07; fork of vmg/sundown.

notes: Better source found: cmark benchmarks.md at tags 0.21.0-0.29.0 carries the full table with methodology and a direct discount row (no chaining needed), so tier raised to B as an independent measurement; benchmark_url, claimed_speedup, workload, hardware corrected.
